passage:
I’ve worked beside Bidisha for four years, and I owe Mr. Anand more than I can say, since he backed me when I was new. So when he told the team to keep the faulty-helmet report “internal” until the audit passed, I nodded like the others.
But a batch of those helmets shipped last week. Someone’s head will be under one, and I keep seeing that.
Bidisha said in the corridor, “Don’t be the one who breaks us.” The word traitor sat in my throat. I said nothing.
I still haven’t decided. Tonight I looked up the ethics line, and I’ve asked for a slot on Monday.
— Rashmi

qa.q: How long has Rashmi worked beside Bidisha?
qa.a: Rashmi has worked beside Bidisha for four years.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi nod along when Mr. Anand said to keep the report internal?
qa.a: Rashmi felt loyal to Mr. Anand, who had backed Rashmi when new, and to the team. Rashmi was also afraid of being seen as a traitor.

qa.q: What small step did Rashmi take after the corridor conversation?
qa.a: Rashmi looked up the ethics line and asked for a slot on Monday. That keeps the choice open and moves toward the people who could be hurt.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have been feeling when saying not to break the team?
qa.a: Bidisha may have been afraid of what exposure would do to the team and its jobs, and may have felt loyalty to the team. The passage shows only the warning.

grounding: Shows a professional pulled between loyalty to the team and a superior and knowing something is wrong, with fear of being called a traitor.

passage:
Mentor note, Friday. Deepika stayed after our review and sat with her hands pressed together. She knows a figure in the client report was changed at director level. She said the director gave her first chance, and the team would call her a traitor. “If I speak up, I’m the one who ends up out,” she said.
I told her the worry was real and did not tell her what to do. I asked whether she wanted to see how the company’s ethics line works, and we read the policy together. She took a copy home.
Next Friday I will check in, and she can tell me as much or as little as she wants.
— Vinita

qa.q: What did Deepika know about the client report?
qa.a: Deepika knew a figure in the report had been changed at director level.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she said she would be the one who ended up out?
qa.a: Deepika was afraid of being labelled a traitor and losing her place. Her pressed hands and the mention of the director's early support show real divided loyalty.

qa.q: What did Vinita do that helped without pushing Deepika?
qa.a: Vinita acknowledged the worry, gave no instructions and offered to go through the ethics line policy together. Deepika took a copy home and kept the choice.

qa.q: How might the team see Deepika if she spoke up?
qa.a: Some might see her as a traitor, which is the fear she names. Others might quietly agree, but the passage does not say.

grounding: Shows a professional torn between loyalty to a director and conscience about a changed figure, and a mentor's support.

passage: In the sugar-mill town near Belagavi, Tejas owed everything to his senior, Mr Hegde. Hegde had hired him, taught him the weighbridge, even come to his sister's wedding. So when Tejas noticed that farmers' cane was being under-weighed by a few kilos every load, and that Hegde signed off on it, his chest went tight. The farmers were people he saw at the chai stall. Lavanya, whose father sold cane to the mill, asked one evening, 'Appa thinks the scale is cheating him. Is it?' Tejas didn't answer. At home he wrote out the readings, then tore up the page. If he reported it, the whole office would call him a traitor, and Hegde would be ruined. If he didn't, farmers like Lavanya's father would keep losing. He sat with both, awake till dawn.

qa.q: What did Tejas notice about the farmers' cane?
qa.a: It was being under-weighed by a few kilos every load.

qa.q: Why did Tejas tear up the page of readings?
qa.a: He felt torn between loyalty and guilt, afraid of being called a traitor and of ruining Mr Hegde.

qa.q: What is one safe next step Tejas could take?
qa.a: Keep a record of the readings and talk quietly to a trusted senior or the cooperative's auditor, so the farmers are protected without Tejas acting alone.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's father feel about the weighbridge?
qa.a: Suspicious and wronged, believing the scale is cheating him, as Lavanya says.

grounding: A young engineer feels real loyalty to a senior and real duty to wronged farmers, and fear of being called a traitor.

passage: Oskar had worked in Chef Brandt's kitchen in Berlin for three years. Brandt had taken him on when no one else would and taught him everything. Tonight Oskar watched Brandt peel the date labels off a tray of chicken and stick on new ones. 'Busy weekend,' Brandt said. 'Nobody gets sick from one day.' Oskar's stomach turned. His friend Yara, at the next station, raised her eyebrows at him. Loyalty pulled one way: Brandt was like an uncle. Conscience pulled the other: a table of schoolchildren had booked for tomorrow. In the walk-in fridge, Yara whispered, 'If you don't, I will.' Oskar took a breath, moved the tray to the waste bin and quietly told Brandt he would not cook it. Brandt stared at him. 'Traitor,' he muttered.

qa.q: What did Chef Brandt do to the tray of chicken?
qa.a: Peeled off the date labels and stuck on new ones.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling in the kitchen?
qa.a: Torn and sick, pulled by loyalty to Brandt, who was like an uncle, and by fear for the schoolchildren.

qa.q: What protective step did Oskar take?
qa.a: He moved the tray to the waste bin and quietly told Brandt he wouldn't cook it, so the food was not served.

qa.q: How might Yara see the situation?
qa.a: Yara sees the danger clearly and is ready to act, pushing Oskar with 'If you don't, I will.'

grounding: A young cook feels loyalty to a mentor and a duty to diners, fears being called a traitor, and acts to protect others.

passage: In the staff room of the Lucknow school, Irfan found the practical-exam mark sheets on Hemant sir's desk, with several low scores neatly changed to higher ones. Hemant sir had mentored him since his first day, covered his classes when his father was ill, and taught him how to handle Class 10. When Irfan asked, Hemant sir sighed. 'Our results decide next year's admissions. We protect each other here. You understand.' Irfan did understand. That was the problem. Walking home, he felt like two people: the one who loved Hemant sir, and the one who thought of the students who had actually earned their marks. Calling it out would make him a traitor in the staff room. Staying quiet would make him part of it. That night he couldn't eat.

qa.q: What had been changed on the practical-exam mark sheets?
qa.a: Several low scores had been changed to higher ones.

qa.q: What did Irfan mean by feeling like two people?
qa.a: He felt torn between loyalty and love for Hemant sir and a guilty sense of duty to students who earned their real marks.

qa.q: What could Irfan do next?
qa.a: Speak privately to Hemant sir again, and if nothing changes, take it to the principal or the board's official channel, keeping a copy of the sheets.

qa.q: How might the students who earned high marks honestly be affected?
qa.a: Their real achievement is blurred, and the results no longer tell the truth about anyone's work.

grounding: A young teacher feels loyalty to a mentor who altered marks and a duty to students, with fear of being called a traitor.

passage:
Mahima,
I need to write this to someone outside the office.
You know Sethi ma'am took me on when no one else would, after I failed my exams twice. The team is like family; we eat from one another's tiffins. Last month I found that the grant for the girls' hostel roof has been moved, quietly, into salaries. On paper the roof is "in progress". In real life, the girls in the top dorm put buckets under the leaks every night.
When I asked, ma'am said, "Vikas, trust me. We'll fix it next quarter." Ravi from accounts told me not to be "the traitor who breaks us".
Both things feel true. I love these people. And thirty girls are sleeping under a leaking roof.
I keep drafting an email to the board and deleting it. I'm scared.
Tell me I'm not crazy.
Vikas

qa.q: What was the grant meant for?
qa.a: The grant was meant for the girls' hostel roof.

qa.q: What is Vikas feeling while drafting and deleting the email?
qa.a: Vikas feels torn and scared: grateful and loyal to Sethi ma'am and the team, but troubled by the girls under the leaking roof.

qa.q: What would you advise Vikas to do next?
qa.a: Write down what was found with dates, talk it through with a trusted adviser outside the office, and use the proper channel, such as the board, instead of waiting for next quarter.

qa.q: What is life like for the girls in the top dorm while this goes on?
qa.a: They put buckets under the leaks every night, bearing the cost of a decision they know nothing about.

grounding: Vikas's letter shows loyalty to a boss and team pulling against conscience, with fear of being called a traitor outweighing duty to those harmed.
